div.p: Let another heap up riches for himself in tawny gold and hold many acres of well-tilled soil, let ceaseless toil terrify him with the enemy near, the blare of the war-trumpet driving sleep from him: let my own poverty lead me through a quiet life, so long as my hearth shines with a steady fire. With my own hand I would set the tender vines in their due season, a countryman, and the tall fruit-trees with practised ease; nor let Hope fail me, but always grant me heaps of grain and rich new wine in a brimming vat. For I pay my reverence, whether a lonely stump in the fields or an old stone at the crossroads bears a garland of flowers, and whatever fruit the new year ripens for me is set, an offering, before the farmer's god. Golden Ceres, for you let there be a crown of grain-ears from our farm, to hang before the temple doors, and let a red guardian be set in the orchard plots, that Priapus may scare the birds with his fierce sickle. You too, Lares, guardians of a field once happy, now poor, receive your offerings. Then a slain heifer purified the countless herds, now a lamb is the small victim of a meagre plot. A lamb shall fall for you, around which the country youth shall shout, "Hail! grant us harvests and good wine." Now, only now, may I live content with little, nor be forever given over to the long road, but shun the rising of the summer Dog-star beneath the shade of a tree, by the streams of running water. Yet at times let me not be ashamed to have held the hoe or to have urged on the lagging oxen with the goad, nor let it irk me to carry home in my arms a lamb or a kid abandoned by its forgetful mother. But you, thieves and wolves, spare my little flock: your spoil must be sought from the great herd. Here it is my custom each year to purify my shepherd and to sprinkle gentle Pales with milk. Be present, gods, and do not scorn the gifts from a poor table nor those from clean earthenware. Of earthenware the ancient countryman first made his cups for himself, and shaped them from pliant clay. I do not long for the riches of my fathers, nor the harvest-yields that the stored grain brought to my forefather of old: a small crop is enough, enough to rest upon a bed if I may, and to ease my limbs upon the accustomed couch. How pleasant, lying there, to hear the wild winds and to hold one's mistress in a tender embrace, or, when the wintry South Wind has poured down its icy waters, to follow sleep untroubled, with the fire to help. Let this be my lot. Let him be rich by right who can endure the fury of the sea and the cheerless rains. O let all the gold and the emeralds in the world perish rather than that any girl should weep over my journeys. It befits you, Messalla, to wage war by land and sea, that your house may display the spoils of the enemy; me the chains of a lovely girl hold bound, and I sit, a doorkeeper, before her unyielding doors. I do not care to be praised, my Delia; so long as I am with you, I ask to be called sluggish and idle. Let me look upon you when my last hour comes, let me hold you, dying, with my failing hand. You will weep, Delia, when I am laid on the bed about to burn, and you will give me kisses mingled with sorrowful tears. You will weep: your heart is not bound with hard iron, nor is there flint within your tender breast. From that funeral no youth, no maiden will be able to bring home eyes that are dry. Do not wound my spirit, Delia, but spare your loosened hair, and spare your tender cheeks. Meanwhile, while the fates allow, let us join our loves: soon Death will come, her head veiled in darkness, soon sluggish age will steal upon us, nor will it be fitting to love or to speak sweet nothings with a grey head. Now must light Venus be courted, while it is no shame to break down doors, and a delight to have started quarrels. Here I am a good general and soldier: you, standards and trumpets, go far away, carry wounds to greedy men, carry them wealth too: I, untroubled, with my store laid up, will look down on riches and look down on hunger.

Let whoever is present keep holy silence: we purify the crops and the fields, as the rite stands handed down from our forefather of old. Bacchus, come, and let the sweet grape hang from your horns, and Ceres, wreathe your temples with corn-ears. On this sacred day let the earth rest, let the ploughman rest, and the heavy work cease, the ploughshare hung up. Loose the straps from the yokes: now at the full mangers the oxen ought to stand, their heads garlanded. Let all things be devoted to the god: let no woman dare to lay her wool-working hand to the day's spinning. You too I bid keep far off, let him withdraw from the altars to whom Venus brought her joys in the night just past. Pure things please the gods above: come in clean garments and with clean hands take up the water of the spring. See how the sacred lamb goes to the gleaming altars, and the white throng behind, their hair bound with olive. Gods of my fathers, we cleanse the fields, we cleanse the husbandmen: drive you the evils from our boundaries, let the crop not cheat the harvest with deceitful blades, let the slower lamb not fear the swift wolves. Then the sleek countryman, trusting in his full fields, will heap great logs upon the blazing hearth, and the crowd of home-born slaves, the good sign of a prosperous farmer, will play and build little huts of twigs before the fire. I pray for what is to come: do you see how, with favourable entrails, the prophetic fibre signals the gods are kindly? Now bring out for me the smoky Falernian of an old consul's year, and loose the bindings of a Chian jar. Let wine grace the day: it is no shame to grow soaked on a festal day and to bear one's wandering feet badly. But let each man, over his cups, drink the health of Messalla, and at every word let the name of the absent one ring out. Messalla, renowned for triumphs over the Aquitanian people, and a victor of great glory to your unshorn forefathers, come hither and breathe favour upon me, while in my song thanks are rendered to the gods of the countryside. I sing of the fields and the gods of the fields. With these for teachers life ceased to drive off hunger with the acorn of the oak: they first taught how to cover with green foliage a little house, its beams set together; they too, men say, were the first to teach the bulls servitude, and to set the wheel beneath the wagon. Then savage ways departed, then the fruit-tree was planted, then the fertile garden drank the watering streams, then the golden grape gave up its juices, pressed by the feet, and sober water was mixed with untroubled wine. The fields bear harvests, when with the heat of the burning star the yearly earth lays down her yellow tresses. In the field the light bee, in springtime, brings flowers to the hive, that, busy, it may fill the combs with sweet honey. The countryman, first sated by the constant plough, sang rustic words to a steady measure and, full-fed, first piped a song upon the dry reed, to recite before the adorned gods, the countryman first, stained with reddening vermilion, Bacchus, led the dances with as-yet-untried art. To him a memorable gift, given from the full sheepfold, a he-goat, leader of the flock, increased his scanty wealth. In the field a boy first made a garland from the spring flowers and set it upon the ancient Lares. In the field too the gleaming ewe bears the soft fleece on her back, to give tender girls their task. Hence women's labour, hence the spinning and the distaff, the spindle that turns the work with the thumb pressed to it: and some weaver, busy at unwearying Minerva's craft, sings, and the loom rings from the beaten warp. Cupid himself, too, is said to have been born among the fields, among the herds, among the untamed mares. There he first practised himself with an untrained bow: ah me, how skilled now are the hands he has! Nor does he aim, as before, at cattle: he longs to pierce girls and to subdue bold men. He has stripped the young man of his wealth, he has bidden the old man speak shameful words at the door of an angry mistress: under his guidance the girl, stealing alone in the dark past the guards who lie there, comes to her young lover, and feels out the path with her feet, suspended in fear, exploring the unseen ways before her with her hand. Ah, wretched are they whom this god harshly oppresses! but happy is he on whom gentle Love softly breathes. Holy one, come to our festive feasts, but lay aside your arrows and put far from here, I pray, your burning torches. Sing you the renowned god, and call him with your voice for the flock: let each man call him aloud for the flock, in secret for himself. Or even aloud, each for himself: for the merry crowd makes its din, and the curved pipe with its Phrygian strain. Make sport: now Night yokes her horses, and the golden stars follow their mother's chariot in a wanton band, and behind comes silent Sleep, wrapped in dusky wings, and the black Dreams with their uncertain step.

The festal Kalends of Roman Mars have come — this was the New Year's Day for our forefathers — and now gifts run everywhere in roving procession through the streets of the city and through its houses. Tell me, Pierian Muses, with what honour she should be presented, my dear Neaera, or, if I am deceived, dear still. Lovely women are won by song, the greedy by a price: let her rejoice, as she deserves, in my verses. But let a saffron parchment wrap the snow-white little book, and let the pumice first trim its grey edges, let fine vellum face the upper ends of the page, so that the lettering may proclaim your name, and let horns be painted between the twin margins: for thus it is fitting to send a finished work, well-adorned. By you, the authors of this song of mine, I pray, and by the Castalian shade and the Pierian pools, go to her house and give her my well-dressed little book, just as it will be: let no colour run from it. She will tell me whether her care for me is mutual, or grown less, or fallen wholly from her heart. But first, as she deserves, give her bountiful greeting, and speak these words in a hushed tone: "This chaste Neaera, your husband once, now your brother, sends to you, and asks that you accept these small gifts, and swears that you are dearer to him than his own marrow, whether you are to be his wife or his sister; but rather his wife: of the hope of that name the pale water of Dis will rob him only when he is dead."

Pour out more wine, and with the wine subdue these fresh sorrows, that sleep may seize the conquered eyes of a weary man, and let no one wake him whose temples are struck deep with much Bacchus, while his unhappy love finds rest. For a cruel watch has been set upon my girl, and the unyielding door is barred fast with a hard bolt. Door of a difficult master, may the rain lash you, may the thunderbolts sent at Jove's command seek you out. Door, now open to me alone, conquered by my complaints, and do not, swinging stealthily on your hinge, give a sound. And if my madness has uttered any curse against you, forgive it: I pray those words may fall on my own head. It is right you should remember the many things I uttered with suppliant voice, when I laid flowery garlands upon your post. You too, Delia, do not timidly cheat your guards, one must be daring: Venus herself helps the brave. She favours whether some youth essays an unfamiliar threshold or a girl unbars the doors with the key set in the lock; she teaches how to creep stealthily from a soft bed, she teaches how to set the foot down without a sound, she teaches how, before the husband's very face, to exchange speaking nods and to hide coaxing words in agreed-upon signs. Nor does she teach this to all, but to those whom no sloth holds back nor any fear forbids to rise in the dark of night. Look, while I wander anxious through the whole city in the dark, . . . she does not let anyone meet me who would wound my body with the sword, or seek plunder by stripping off my cloak. Whoever is held by love, let him go safe and sacred wherever he will: it does not befit him to fear ambush. The sluggish cold of a winter's night does not harm me, nor does the rain when it falls in floods of water. This hardship does not hurt me, if only Delia unbars her door and silently calls me with the snap of her finger. Spare your eyes, whether man or woman comes to meet me: Venus wishes her thefts to be concealed. Do not frighten me with the noise of your feet, nor ask my name, nor bring gleaming torches near. And if anyone has caught sight of us unawares, let him hide it and by all the gods deny that he remembers: for whoever has been a babbler shall learn that Venus was born of blood and sprung from the raging sea. Yet not even him will your husband believe, as the truthful witch promised me by her magic ministry. I have seen her draw down the stars from the sky, she turns the course of a rushing river with her spell, she splits the ground with her chant and calls up the Shades from their tombs and summons the bones from the warm pyre; now she holds the infernal hosts fast with her magic shriek, now bids them, sprinkled with milk, draw back their step. When she pleases, she drives the clouds from a gloomy sky, when she pleases, she calls up snows in a summer world. She alone is said to possess the evil herbs of Medea, she alone to have tamed the fierce hounds of Hecate. She has composed for me chants by which you may deceive him: sing them three times, and after the chant spit three times. He will be able to believe nothing about us from anyone, not even his own eyes, should he see us himself upon the soft couch. Yet you must keep from others: for all else he will perceive, but of me alone he himself will perceive nothing. What then, am I to believe? This same woman said she could loose my love with her chants or her herbs, and she purified me with torches, and on a clear night a dark victim fell before the magic gods. I prayed not that my love should wholly depart, but that it be returned, nor would I wish to be able to do without you. He was a man of iron who, when he might have had you, preferred, fool, to follow plunder and arms. Let him drive the conquered hosts of the Cilicians before him, let him pitch his martial camp on captured ground, all wound about with silver, all with gold, let him sit, a sight to behold, upon his swift horse, if only with you, my Delia, I might yoke my oxen and pasture my flock upon the accustomed hill, and hold you, while it is allowed, in my tender arms, then soft would be my sleep on the unploughed ground. What good is it to lie upon a Tyrian couch without love returned, when night must be passed awake in weeping? For then neither feathers nor embroidered coverlets nor the sound of gentle water could bring on sleep. Have I violated the power of great Venus with a word, and does my impious tongue now pay the penalty? Am I charged with having approached the seats of the gods, unclean, and torn the garlands from the holy hearths? If I have deserved it, I would not hesitate to fall before the temples and to give kisses to the hallowed thresholds, I would not hesitate to crawl on my knees, a suppliant, over the ground and to beat my wretched head against the sacred post. But you who laugh gladly at my misfortunes, take care for yourself soon: the god will not rage against one man forever. I have seen one who had mocked the wretched loves of the young in old age bow his neck beneath the chains of Venus and frame coaxing words for himself in a trembling voice and try to arrange his white hair with his hands, nor was he ashamed to stand before the doors of his dear girl or to detain her maid in the middle of the forum. Him the boy, him the youth crowds about in a packed throng, and each one spits into his own soft bosom. But spare me, Venus: my mind serves you, always devoted: why, harsh one, do you burn your own harvests?

Let us speak words of good omen: the Birthday comes to the altars: whoever is present, man and woman, keep favourable silence. Let pious incense burn upon the hearths, let those perfumes burn that the tender Arab sends from his rich land. Let the Genius himself be present, to see his own honours, let soft garlands adorn his holy hair. Let his temples drip with pure spikenard, let him be sated with cake and soaked with wine, and let him grant you, Cornutus, whatever you ask. Come now (why do you delay? he has granted it) ask. I prophesy you will pray for the faithful love of a wife: already, I think, the very gods have learned this by heart. Nor would you choose for yourself whatever fields, the whole world over, the brave countryman ploughs with his sturdy ox, nor whatever of jewels is born among the favoured Indians, where the wave of the Eastern sea grows red. The vows are answered: O may Love fly here on rustling wings and bring the golden bonds of wedlock, bonds to last forever, until slow old age brings on the wrinkles and dyes the hair grey. May this birthday come with happy omen and grant offspring, and may a fresh band of children play before your feet.

He who first tore from a youth the girl dear to him, and the youth dear to the girl, that man was iron; and hard too was he who could bear so great a grief, and live, when his wife was snatched away. I am not strong in this; this patience is not in my nature: grief breaks even brave hearts; nor am I ashamed to speak the truth, and to confess that weariness has been born of my life, which has endured so many ills. Therefore, when I shall have been changed into a thin shade and the black ash covers my white bones, let Neaera come before my pyre, her long hair unbound, and let her weep, mournful, before my pyre; but let her come accompanied by her dear mother's grief: let this one mourn for her son-in-law, that one for her husband. Having first spoken before my Manes and prayed for my soul, and bathed their pious hands first in water, the bones, the only part of my body that will survive, they will gather, white, girt in black raiment, and first sprinkle the gathered remains with aged wine, then too cleanse them with snow-white milk, after this dry up the moisture with linen cloths and lay them, dried, in their marble home. There let the wares that rich Panchaia sends and the Eastern Arabs, and rich Assyria, and tears in memory of me, be poured out in the same place: so would I wish to be laid, when I am turned to bones. But let an inscription declare the mournful cause of my death, and mark these verses on the much-frequented front: HERE LYGDAMUS LIES: GRIEF AND LONGING FOR NEAERA, HIS WIFE SNATCHED FROM HIM, WERE THE CAUSE OF HIS DEATH.

You will go, Messalla, over the Aegean waves without me, O may you and your company remember me. Phaeacia holds me sick in an unknown land, only hold back your greedy hands, black Death, I pray. Hold back, dark Death, I beg: here I have no mother to gather my burnt bones into her mournful bosom, no sister to give Assyrian perfumes to my ashes and weep before the tomb with loosened hair, Delia is nowhere; she, when she sent me from the city, is said to have first consulted all the gods. Three times she drew the sacred lots of the boy: three times the boy brought her back sure omens from the three. All foretold my return: yet she was never frightened from weeping and looking back upon my journey. I myself, her comforter, though I had already given my last commands, kept anxiously seeking out the slow delays. Either I made excuse of the birds or of dire omens, or that the sacred day of Saturn had detained me. O how often, having begun my journey, did I say my stumbling foot had given evil signs at the gate! Let no one dare to depart against Love's will, or let him know that he set out with a god forbidding it. What now does your Isis profit me, Delia, what profit me those bronze rattles so often shaken by your hand, or that, while you piously tended the rites, you bathed in purity and—I remember—slept apart upon an unstained bed? Now, goddess, now come to my aid—for that you can heal many a painted tablet upon your temple walls declares— that my Delia, paying the vows she promised, may sit before the sacred doors, robed in linen, and twice a day, her hair loosened, be bound to sing your praises, conspicuous in the Pharian throng. But let it be my lot to honour my fathers' household gods and to render the monthly incense to the ancient Lar. How well men lived when Saturn was king, before the earth was opened up into long roads! Not yet had the pine despised the dark-blue waves, nor offered its swelling sail to the winds, nor had the wandering sailor, seeking gain in unknown lands, loaded his ship with foreign merchandise. In that age no strong bull bent to the yoke, no horse champed the bit with its broken-in mouth, no house had doors, no stone was fixed in the fields to mark out the boundaries of the land with certain limits. The oaks themselves gave honey, and of their own accord the ewes brought their udders of milk to meet the carefree folk. There was no battle-line, no anger, no wars, nor had the savage smith forged the sword with his pitiless craft. Now, under Jove as master, there is slaughter and wounds forever, now the sea, now a thousand sudden roads to death. Spare me, father. No perjuries make me, the timid one, afraid, no impious words spoken against the holy gods. But if I have now completed my appointed years, let a stone stand above my bones with these words inscribed: "Here lies Tibullus, consumed by pitiless death, while he followed Messalla over land and sea." But me, because I have always been pliant to tender Love, Venus herself will lead to the Elysian fields. There dances and songs flourish, and roaming far and wide the birds sweetly sound their slender-throated song, the untilled field bears cassia, and over all the meadows the kindly earth blooms with fragrant roses; and a band of youths mingled with tender girls plays, and Love forever joins the fray. There is every lover to whom rapacious death has come, and he wears garlands of myrtle in his marked-out hair. But the place of the wicked lies hidden in deep night, buried, around which the black rivers roar: and Tisiphone, with savage snakes for unkempt hair, rages, and the impious throng flees here and there. Then at the gate black Cerberus, with serpents on his mouth, hisses and keeps watch before the brazen doors. There the guilty limbs of Ixion, who dared to assault Juno, are whirled upon the swift wheel, and Tityos, stretched over nine acres of ground, feeds the unwearying birds with his black entrails. Tantalus is there, and pools around him, but the water deserts his keen thirst just as he is about to drink, and the daughters of Danaus, because they offended the powers of Venus, carry the waters of Lethe into hollow jars. There let him be, whoever has violated my loves and wished long campaigns upon me. But you, I pray, remain chaste, and let a guardian crone sit ever watchful, a keeper of your holy modesty. Let her tell you tales, and by the set lamp draw out the long threads from her full distaff, while around her the girl, bent over her heavy task of wool, little by little, weary, gives over her work to sleep. Then let me come suddenly, with no one to announce me first, but let me seem to come to you, sent from heaven. Then, just as you are, your long hair in disarray, run barefoot, Delia, to meet me. This I pray: may radiant Dawn bring us that shining morning star upon her rosy steeds.

The country and the farmhouses hold my girl, Cornutus: iron-hearted, alas, is whoever stays in the city. Venus herself has now migrated into the broad fields, and Love learns the rustic words of the ploughman. O, when I might look upon my mistress, how bravely there would I turn the rich soil with the sturdy hoe and follow the curved plough in the farmer's way, while the barren oxen break up the fields for sowing! Nor would I complain that the sun scorched my slender limbs, or that the broken blister chafed my tender hands. Handsome Apollo too pastured the bulls of Admetus, and neither his lyre nor his unshorn hair availed him, nor could he heal his cares with health-giving herbs: love had overcome all that the healing art could do. The god himself was wont to drive the cows from the stalls . . . and to teach how to curdle the fresh milk with rennet, and how the milky liquid hardened with the mixture. Then the basket was woven of the light osier of the rush, and a wandering way for the whey was made through the meshes. O how often, while he carried a calf through the fields, men say his sister, meeting him, blushed! O how often, while he sang in the deep valley, the bulls dared to break his learned songs with their lowing! Often leaders sought oracles in time of anxious trouble, and the crowd came home from the temples unanswered: often Latona grieved to see in disorder the sacred hair that the stepmother herself had once admired. Whoever saw his unadorned head and his loosened locks would ask for the hair of Phoebus. Where now, Phoebus, is your Delos, where Delphic Pytho? Surely Love bids you dwell in a humble cottage. Happy were they of old, when, men say, the eternal gods were not ashamed to serve Venus openly. A byword he is now: but whoever has a girl for his care would rather be a byword than a god without love. But you, whoever you are, whom with cheerless brow Cupid commands that your camp should be in our house . . . the iron age praises not love but plunder: yet plunder has wrought many evils. Plunder girt the savage battle-lines with discordant arms: hence blood, hence slaughter and death came nearer. Plunder bade men double their perils on the wandering sea, when it gave warlike beaks to the unsteady ships. The plunderer longs to seize on measureless plains, that he may pasture many acres with countless sheep: one to whom foreign marble is a care, and through the city's uproar a thousand columns are carried on sturdy yokes, and a mole encloses the untamed sea, so that within the lazy fish may not heed the threats of winter at hand. But for me let Samian crockery draw out the merry feasts, and the smooth clay shaped on the Cuman wheel. Alas, alas, I see that girls rejoice in rich men: now let the plunder come, if Venus desires wealth: that my Nemesis may flow with luxury and walk through the city, conspicuous in my gifts. Let her wear the fine robes that a Coan woman has woven, and arranged with golden stripes: let her have dark attendants, whom the sun of India scorches and the fire stains as the horses are driven near: let Africa and Tyre vie to furnish her choice colours, the scarlet and the purple. I speak of what is known: he holds a kingdom himself, whom often the barbarous platform forced to bear his chalked feet. But for you, hard crop, who lead my Nemesis away from the city, may Earth render no seeds with any faith. And you, tender Bacchus, planter of the joyous grape, you too, Bacchus, leave the accursed vats. It is not allowed unpunished to hide lovely girls in the cheerless fields: your new wine is not worth so much, father. O perish the harvests, if only there be no girls in the country: let the acorn nourish, and water be drunk in the ancient way. The acorn nourished the men of old, and everywhere they always loved: what harm did it do to have no furrows sown? Then to those on whom Love breathed, gentle Venus openly offered her joys in the shady valley. There was no guard, no door to shut out the grieving lover: if it is right, I pray, that custom of old, return. . . . let them cover their rough bodies with shaggy clothing. Now if my girl is shut away, if rare is my chance to see her, alas the wretchedness, what good is it that the toga hangs loose? Lead me on: at my mistress's command I will furrow the fields: I do not refuse the chains and the lashes.

What good is it, Neaera, to have filled heaven with vows and to have given coaxing incense with many a prayer, not that I might come forth from a threshold of marble roof, distinguished and conspicuous in a famous house, or that my bulls might break the many acres anew and the kindly earth might give great harvests, but that I might share with you the joys of a long life and that my old age might fall in your embrace, then, when, my measured span of light fulfilled, I should be forced to go, naked, on the boat of Lethe? For what good to me is the heavy weight of rich gold, or if a thousand oxen cleave my fertile fields? What good is a house propped on Phrygian columns, or yours, Taenarus, or yours, Carystus, and groves within the houses imitating sacred woods, and gilded beams and a floor of marble? Or what good is the shell that is gathered on the Erythraean shore, and the wool dyed with Sidonian purple, and what besides the people marvel at? In those things there is envy: the common crowd loves much that is false. The minds and cares of men are not eased by wealth, nor does Fortune govern her seasons by her own law. Let poverty with you be pleasant to me, Neaera: but without you I want no gifts of kings. O the snow-white light that could give you back to me! O the day thrice and four times happy for me! But if, against all the vows that are made for a sweet return, my god should listen with averted ear, neither kingdoms please me, nor the gold-bearing Lydian river, nor what wealth the round world of lands sustains. Let others desire these; let it be mine, in poor estate, to be able to enjoy a dear wife untroubled. Be present and favour my timid vows, daughter of Saturn, and favour them, Cyprian goddess, borne upon your shell. But if the fates deny my return, and the cheerless Sisters, who draw out the threads and spin what is to be, let lurid Orcus, rich in his idle water, call me to the vast rivers and the black marsh.

"So may shady shelter be yours, Priapus, that neither suns nor snows may harm your head: what skill of yours has captured the handsome boys? Surely no beard gleams on you, nor is your hair well-tended, naked you endure the cold of the wintry frost, naked the dry season of the summer Dog-star." So I; then the rustic son of Bacchus answered, the god armed with his curved sickle, thus to me: "O flee from trusting yourself to the tender throng of boys, for they always have cause to justify love. This one pleases because he reins his horse with a tight bridle, this one because he cleaves the calm water with his snowy breast, this one has captured you because bold daring is his; but on that one maidenly modesty sits before his tender cheeks. But do not let weariness seize you, if at first by chance he refuses: little by little he will give his neck beneath the yoke. Long time has taught man to make lions obey, long time has worn away the rocks with soft water; the year ripens the grapes on the sunny hillsides, the year drives round the bright stars in their fixed turn. And do not fear to swear: the winds carry off the perjuries of Venus, making them void, across the lands and the surface of the seas. Great thanks to Jove: the father himself forbade that any oath should hold good which foolish love had sworn in its eagerness, and Dictynna lets you affirm by her arrows unpunished, and Minerva by her hair. But if you are slow, you will go astray: youth passes. How quickly the unwearying day stands still and returns, how quickly the earth loses its bright colours, how quickly the tall poplar loses its lovely leaves! How low he lies, when the fates of feeble age have come, the horse that was first sent from the Elean barrier! I have seen a young man, when his later years pressed upon him, lamenting that he had let his foolish days slip by. Cruel gods! the serpent, renewed, sloughs off its years, but the fates have granted no respite to beauty. For Bacchus and Phoebus alone is youth eternal, for unshorn hair befits both gods. You, in whatever your boy may wish to attempt, give way: love conquers most by yielding. And do not refuse to go as his companion, though the road be long and the Dog-star scorch the fields with parching thirst, though the rain-bringing rainbow, fringing the sky with painted purple, foretell the coming downpour. Or if he wishes to go over the dark-blue waves by ship, yourself drive the light vessel through the waters with the oar. And do not regret having taken up hard labours or having chafed your unaccustomed hands with toil, nor, if he wishes to ring the deep valleys with snares, let your shoulders, so you may please him, refuse to bear the nets. If he wants weapons, you will try to play with a light hand: often you will leave your side bare, that he may win. Then he will be gentle to you, then you may snatch dear kisses: he will resist, but yet will give them as he should. First he will give them snatched, then he himself will bring them when you ask, later he may even wish to twine himself about your neck. Alas, how badly this age now handles its wretched arts: now the tender boy has grown used to wanting gifts. But you who first taught how to sell love, whoever you are, may a heavy stone press upon your bones. Love the Muses, boys, and the learned poets, nor let golden gifts surpass the Muses. By song the purple lock of Nisus lives: were there no songs, the ivory would not have gleamed upon the shoulder of Pelops. Whom the Muses tell of shall live, while earth bears oaks, while heaven bears stars, while the river carries its waters. But he who does not heed the Muses, who sells love, let him follow the chariot of Idaean Ops and wander, filling three hundred cities, and cut off his worthless members to the Phrygian measures. Venus herself wishes there to be room for coaxing words: for suppliant complaints, for wretched weeping, she shows her favour." These things the god uttered for me to sing to Titius, but Titius's wife forbids him to remember them. Let him obey his own; but do you make me famous as your master, you whom a sly boy holds in misery with all his craft. Each has his own glory: let lovers who are scorned consult me: my door stands open to all. The time will come when, as I bear the precepts of Venus, an eager throng of youths will escort me, an old man. Alas, alas, how Marathus torments me with lingering love! My arts fail me, and my tricks fail too. Spare me, boy, I beg, lest I become a shameful story, when they laugh at my empty teachings.

Here I see slavery and a mistress ready for me: now, that ancestral freedom of mine, farewell. But cheerless slavery is given, and I am held in chains, and Love never loosens the bonds for my misery, and whether I have earned something or sinned in nothing, he burns me. I burn, alas! Take away your torches, cruel girl. O that I might not be able to feel such pains, how much rather would I be a stone on the icy mountains, or stand a crag exposed to the raging winds, which the wave of the vast sea, wrecking ships, might beat upon! Now both the day is bitter and the shadow of night more bitter: for all the hours are steeped in cheerless gall. Neither elegies avail nor Apollo, author of song: she forever demands a price with her hollow hand. Go far off, Muses, if you are no help to a lover: I do not court you that wars may be sung, nor do I tell of the paths of the Sun, or how, when she has filled her orb, the Moon runs back, her horses turned about. I seek easy access to my mistress through songs: go far off, Muses, if those songs have no power. But I must get gifts by murder and crime, that I may not lie weeping before her closed house: or I will snatch the offerings hung up in the holy shrines: but Venus before all the rest must be wronged by me. She prompts the evil deed and gives me a rapacious mistress: let her feel my sacrilegious hands. O perish whoever gathers the green emeralds and stains the snowy sheep with Tyrian purple. This adds reasons for greed, and the Coan robe, and the bright shell from the Red Sea, to girls. These have made them wicked: hence the door has felt the key, and the dog has begun to be a guardian of the threshold. But if you bring a great price, the guard is overcome, the keys do not bar you, and the dog itself is silent. Alas, whatever god gave beauty to a greedy woman, what a blessing he brought, with so many evils! Hence weeping and quarrels resound, this is the very cause that Love now wanders, an infamous god. But you who shut out, for a price, the lovers you have conquered, may wind and fire snatch away the riches you have gathered: nay, may the young men gladly watch your house ablaze, nor let anyone diligently add water to the flame. Or if death should come to you, there will be none to mourn, none to bring a gift to your cheerless funeral. But the good woman, who was not greedy, though she had lived a hundred years, will be wept before the blazing pyre: and some old man, revering his loves of long ago, will give yearly garlands to the raised mound and, departing kindly, will say, "Rest in peace, and may the earth lie light above your untroubled bones." True things indeed I warn of, but what do true things profit me? Her law is the one by which I must observe my love. Nay more, should she bid me sell my ancestral seat, go under her command and under the auction-sign, my Lares. Whatever Circe has, whatever poison Medea, whatever herbs the Thessalian land bears, and what, when Venus breathes love into the untamed herds, the hippomanes drips from the loins of the lustful mare— if only my Nemesis look upon me with a calm face, though she mix a thousand other herbs, I will drink them.

May the gods bring better things, and may they not be true for me, the dreams that the worst of sleep brought last night. Go far away, idle visions, and turn aside your false sights, cease wishing to seek belief in us. The gods give true warning, the entrails approved by Tuscan men give true warning, the messengers of fortune to come; but rash dreams make sport in the deceitful night and bid timid minds fear what is false; and the race of men, born to cares, appeases the omens of night with pious meal and leaping salt! And yet, however it be, whether the gods wish him to be truly warned, or to trust a lying dream, let Lucina make the night's fears empty and grant that I have feared, in vain, for the undeserving, if my mind is guilty of no shameful deed and no impious tongue has wronged the great gods. Now Night, having measured the airy world with her black team, had bathed her wheels in the dark-blue stream, nor had the god that helps the sick mind lulled me to sleep: Sleep fails before troubled houses. At last, when Phoebus looked out from the height of his rising, late rest pressed down my drooping eyes. Then a youth, his temples bound with chaste laurel, was seen to set his foot in my dwelling. No age of those before bore anything more beautiful than he, nor did any house of heroes bear his like. His unshorn locks flowed down his long neck, his myrtle-scented hair dripped with Syrian dew. His was such radiance as the Latonian Moon shows forth, and a rosy colour upon his snow-white body, as when the maiden, first led to her young husband, stains her tender cheeks with a blushing face, and as when girls weave white lilies with amaranth, and the bright apples redden in autumn. A robe of such a hue seemed to play about his feet: for this was the garment on his gleaming body. A work of rare art, gleaming with tortoise-shell and gold, a chattering lyre hung at his left side. This, as he first came, he tuned with an ivory plectrum and gave forth happy songs with his sounding voice; but after his fingers had spoken together with his voice, he uttered these cheerless words in a sweet measure: "Hail, care of the gods: for rightly Phoebus and Bacchus and the Pierian Maids favour the chaste poet; but Bacchus, the offspring of Semele, and the learned sisters do not know how to tell what the next hour will bring; but to me the father granted to be able to see the laws of fate and what is to come in the ages of the future; therefore receive what I say, no lying prophet, and what I, the Cynthian god, bear to you with truthful lips. She who is dear to you as no daughter is to her mother, as no lovely girl is to her eager husband, for whom you trouble the powers of heaven with vows, who lets no day of yours pass untroubled and, when Sleep has veiled you in his dusky cloak, deceives you, idle, with images of the night, Neaera the lovely, celebrated in your songs, would rather be another man's girl, and her impious mind drives her diverse cares, nor does Neaera rejoice, a bride, in a chaste home. Ah, cruel race, and woman, a faithless name! Ah, perish whatever woman has learned to deceive her man! But she can be turned: their minds are changeable; do but stretch out your arms with much faith. Cruel Love taught us to attempt mighty labours, cruel Love taught us to be able to endure the lash. That I once pastured the snow-white heifers of Admetus is no tale made up for an idle jest; then I could not delight in the sounding lyre nor render with my voice sounds like its strings, but I rehearsed a song upon the clear-toned reed, I, that son of Latona and of Jove. You do not know what love is, young man, if you refuse to bear a harsh mistress and a cruel wedlock. Therefore do not hesitate to bring coaxing complaints to bear: hard hearts are conquered by soft prayer. But if the oracles in the sacred temples sing true, report these words to her in my name: the Delian himself promises you this marriage; happy in this, cease to wish for another man." He spoke, and idle sleep ebbed from my body. Ah, may I never be able to see such ills! Nor could I believe that you held vows contrary to mine, nor that so great a crime was in your heart: for neither the waters of the vast sea bore you, nor the Chimaera rolling flame from her savage mouth, nor the dog girt with a serpent-coil on his back, who has three tongues and a triple head, nor Scylla, her maiden shape girt about with dogs, nor did a savage lioness bear you conceived, nor the barbarous land of Scythia or the dreadful Syrtis, but a cultured home, not to be dwelt in by the harsh, and a mother gentlest far before all others, and a father than whom no other is more loving. May the god turn these cruel dreams to better and bid the warm South Winds bear them away unfulfilled.

I was harsh, and I said I bore our parting well, but now that brave boast is far from me. For I am driven like a swift top whirled across the level ground by the lash, which a nimble boy spins with practised art. Burn the wild one and torment him, that after this he may not wish to say anything proud: tame these defiant words. Yet spare me, by the bonds of our stolen bed, by Venus I beg, and by the head laid beside mine. It was I who, when you lay worn out with grievous sickness, am said to have snatched you back by my vows, and I myself purified you all around with clean sulphur, when the crone had chanted her magic song before; I myself made provision that cruel dreams might not be able to harm, with the holy meal thrice consecrated; I myself, veiled with the woollen fillet and my tunic loosened, made nine vows to Trivia in the silent night. All these I paid in full: now another enjoys your love, and that fortunate man profits by my prayers. But for myself I imagined a happy life, if you were spared, madman that I was, but the god refused. "I shall till the fields, and my Delia shall be there to guard the grain, while the threshing-floor beats out the harvest in the warm sun, or she shall keep for me the grapes in the brimming vats and the white new wine pressed by the swift foot; she will grow used to counting the flock, used to having the chattering home-born slave play in the lap of his loving mistress. She will know how to bring to the farmer's god the grape for the vines, the ears for the crop, the feast for the flock. Let her rule them all, let all be in her care, and let it please me to be nothing in the whole house. Here my Messalla will come, for whom Delia shall pluck sweet apples from choice trees; and, reverencing so great a man, let her diligently attend to him, let her prepare for him, and herself, as servant, carry the feast." These things I imagined for myself, which now the East and South winds scatter as vain vows among the perfumed Armenians. Often I tried to drive away my cares with wine, but grief had turned all the wine to tears. Often I held another woman, but just as I came to the joys, Venus reminded me of my mistress and forsook me. Then the woman, departing, said I was bewitched —she is ashamed, and tells how my girl knows unspeakable arts. She does not do this with words, but with her face and her tender arms my girl bewitches, and with her golden hair. Such once to Haemonian Peleus was Thetis, the dark-blue Nereid, borne on a bridled fish. These things have harmed me, that this girl has a wealthy lover; the cunning bawd has come to my ruin. May she eat bloody feasts, and with gory mouth drink cheerless cups mingled with much gall; may the souls of the dead flit about her, lamenting their own fates, forever, and the screech-owl sing from her roof; may she, frenzied, driven by goading hunger, seek out herbs upon the graves and the bones left by savage wolves, may she run with naked loins and howl through the cities, and behind her may a fierce pack of dogs drive her from the crossroads. It shall come to pass: the god gives signs; there are powers that watch the lover, and Venus rages, abandoned in defiance of her just law. But you, as soon as you can, abandon the precepts of the rapacious witch, for every love is conquered by gifts. A poor man will always be at hand, a poor man will be first to come to you and will cling fast to your tender side, a poor man, a faithful companion in the dense crowd of the throng, will lend his hands and make a way for you, a poor man will lead you secretly to your hidden friends and will himself take the bindings from your snowy foot. Alas, I sing in vain, nor does the door, won over by words, open: it must be struck with a full hand. But you who are now preferred, fear my fate: fickle Fortune turns upon the swift orb of her wheel. Not in vain does someone even now stand fast upon the threshold, attentive, and again and again look about and retreat, and pretend to pass the house, then soon comes hurrying back, and alone, before the very doors, keeps clearing his throat. I know not what stealthy love is preparing. Use your time, I beg, while you may: your boat floats on flowing water.

Phoebus, show favour: a new priest enters your temples: come hither with your lyre and your songs. Now, I pray, strike the sounding strings with your thumb, now turn your words to my praises. Yourself, your temples bound with the triumphal laurel, come to your rites, while they heap the altars. But come gleaming and beautiful: now put on the robe laid aside, now comb well your long hair, such as men recall you sang the praises of victorious Jove, when Saturn the king had been put to flight. You see from afar what is to come, to you the augur, devoted, knows well what fate the prophetic bird sings; you rule the lots, through you the soothsayer foresees, when the god has marked the slippery entrails with signs; with you for guide the Sibyl never deceived the Romans, she who sings the hidden fates in six-foot verse. Phoebus, let Messalinus touch the sacred scrolls of the prophetess, and teach him yourself, I pray, what she sings. She gave the oracles to Aeneas, after he, men say, had borne up his father and his rescued Lares and believed Rome would not be, when, mournful, from the deep he looked back upon Ilium and its burning gods. (Romulus had not yet shaped the walls of the eternal city, not to be dwelt in by his fellow Remus; but then the cattle grazed upon the grassy Palatine and humble huts stood on the citadel of Jove. There, dripping with milk, was Pan beneath the shade of the holm-oak, and Pales made of wood with a rustic pruning-knife, and on a tree hung the wandering shepherd's votive offering, the chattering pipe sacred to the woodland god, the pipe whose rows of reed grow ever shorter: for the reed is joined with wax, ever smaller. But where the region of the Velabrum stretches open, a little skiff used to go through the shallows, the water beaten by the oar. Often a girl, on a festal day, to please the wealthy master of the flock, was carried thence to her young lover, with whom returned the gifts of the fruitful country, cheese and the white lamb of a snowy ewe.) "Tireless Aeneas, brother of fluttering Love, who bear the Trojan rites on your fugitive ships, now Jupiter assigns you the Laurentine fields, now the welcoming land calls your wandering Lares. There you will be holy, when the revered water of Numicus has sent you, a deified hero, to the gods in heaven. Lo, Victory flutters above your weary ships; at last the proud goddess comes to the Trojans. Lo, the fires of the Rutulian camp gleam for me: now I foretell your death, barbarous Turnus. Before my eyes is the Laurentine fort and the wall of Lavinium, and Alba Longa, founded by Ascanius the leader. You too I now see, Ilia, priestess to please Mars, who deserted the Vestal hearths, your stolen embraces, your fillets lying low, and the arms of the eager god left upon the banks. Graze now, bulls, the herbage on the seven hills while you may: here will soon be the place of a great city. Rome, your name is fated to rule the lands, wherever Ceres looks down from heaven on her own fields, both where the risings of the Sun lie open and where, with flowing waves, the river bathes the panting horses of the Sun. Troy indeed will then marvel at herself and say to herself that you took good counsel for her over so long a journey. I sing what is true: so may I forever feed, unharmed, upon the sacred laurel, and may my virginity be eternal." These things the prophetess sang, and called you, Phoebus, to herself, and tossed her flowing hair before her face.— Whatever Amalthea, whatever Marpesian Herophile said, what the Greek Phyto warned, and the lots that the Tiburtine sang along the sacred Anio's streams and carried unwetted in her bosom— these foretold that comets would be evil signs of war, that much stone would rain down upon the lands. And they say that trumpets and clashing arms were heard in the sky, and that the groves foretold the flight to come: the cloudy year itself saw the Sun fail of his light and yoke his pale horses: and the images of the gods shed warm tears, and oxen, speaking, gave warning of the fates beforehand. These things had been of old: but you now gentle, Apollo, plunge the portents beneath the untamed seas, and let the laurel, kindled in the sacred flames, crackle well, that the year may be lucky and blessed by that omen. When the laurel has given good signs, rejoice, you farmers; Ceres will fill out your granaries full with corn-ears, and the countryman, smeared with new wine, will strike the grapes with his foot, until the jars and the great vats fail: and the shepherd, soaked with wine, will sing his festal Palilia: then, away from the stalls, keep far off, wolves. He, made drunk by custom, will kindle the heaps of light stubble and leap across the sacred flames. And the matron will bear offspring, and the child will snatch kisses from his parent, gripping his ears, nor will it weary the grandfather to keep watch over his little grandson and, an old man, to speak baby-words with the boy. Then the young people, having served the god, will recline upon the grass, where the light shade of an ancient tree falls, or they will stretch awnings from their garments, bound with garlands, and the goblet itself will stand crowned. And each man will heap high for himself the feast and the festal tables of turf, and a couch of turf. Here a young man, drunk, will heap curses on his girl, which afterwards he would wish unsaid by his vows: for that fierce one, sober, will weep the same and swear that he was out of his mind. By your leave let the bow perish, let the arrows perish, Phoebus, only let Love wander unarmed upon the earth. A good art it is: but after Cupid took up his weapons for himself, alas, alas, to how many has that art brought harm! And to me especially: for a year I lie wounded and (I cherish my sickness, since the very pain delights me) I sing always of Nemesis, without whom no verse of mine can find words or the proper measures. But you—for the guardianship of the gods protects poets— I forewarn you, girl, spare the sacred bard, that I may celebrate Messalinus, when he bears the spoils of war before his chariot, the conquered towns, himself wearing the laurel: bound with rustic laurel, the soldier will sing "Hail, great triumph!" with a loud voice. Then let my Messalla give the loyal crowd their spectacle, and let his father applaud as the chariot passes by. Grant this: so may your hair, Phoebus, be unshorn, so may your sister be chaste for you forever.

You it holds, the water that flows from Etruscan springs, water not to be approached beneath the summer Dog-star, but now, in springtime, nearest to the sacred waters of Baiae, when the earth unbends itself in the purple spring. But to me Persephone announces the black hour: spare to harm an undeserving youth, goddess. I have not boldly attempted to teach the rites of the praiseworthy goddess, not to be profaned by any of men, nor has my hand steeped my cups with deadly juices nor given crushed poisons to anyone, nor have I, a sacrilegious man, set fires to the temples, nor do unspeakable deeds trouble my heart, nor, plotting the quarrels of a maddened mind, have I loosed impious words against the hostile gods. And not yet has grey harmed my black hair, nor has bent old age come with slow foot: my parents saw my birthday first when both consuls fell by an equal fate. What pleasure is it to rob the vine of its growing grapes and to pluck the new-born fruit with a harsh hand? Spare me, you who hold the pale waters, gods allotted the third, the harsh kingdom. Let it be mine one day to know the Elysian fields, the boat of Lethe and the Cimmerian pools, when my face shall grow pale with wrinkled age and, an old man, I tell of olden times to boys. And O that I might be frightened, all in vain, by an empty fever! But my limbs have languished for thrice five days. But for you the powers of the Tuscan water are celebrated, and the easy wave is driven by your supple hand. Live happy, and live mindful of me, whether I shall be, or the fates wish that I have been. Meanwhile promise black beasts to Dis and cups of snow-white milk mingled with wine.

Always, to lure me on, you offer me coaxing looks, but afterwards, Love, you are cheerless and harsh to my misery. What cruelty have you to do with me? Or is it great glory that a god has laid an ambush for a mortal? For nets are spread for me: now Delia in secret, in the silent night, cunningly cherishes I know not whom. She indeed denies it many times over, but it is hard to believe: just so she denies me utterly to her husband. I myself, wretched, taught her by what means she might trick her guards: alas, alas, now I am crushed by my own art. Now she has learned to feign reasons to sleep alone, now she can turn the door on its silent hinge. Then I gave her juices and herbs by which the bruise might fade that mutual love makes with the pressed-in tooth. But you, careless husband of a deceitful girl, keep watch on me too, that she may do no wrong. Beware lest she throng with young men in much talk, nor lie with her breast bared and her dress loose, nor deceive you with a nod, nor draw the wine with her finger and trace signs upon the round of the table. Fear her, however often she goes out, whether she says she goes to see the rites of the Good Goddess, which no man may approach. But if you would trust me, I alone would follow her to the altars; then I should not need to fear for my own eyes. Often, as if I were examining her gems and her signet, I remember I touched her hand on that pretext; often I brought sleep upon you with wine, but I myself drank the sober cups, victorious, with water poured in beneath. I did not wrong you knowingly: forgive me, who confess it, Love commanded: who would bear arms against the gods? I am the one—nor will I now be ashamed to tell the truth— at whom your dog barked all night long. What need have you of a tender wife? If you do not know how to keep your blessings, in vain is the key in the door. She holds you, but sighs for other, absent loves and pretends that her head has suddenly begun to ache. But entrust her to me for keeping: I do not refuse the cruel lashes, I do not shrink from chains upon my feet. Then keep far off, whoever dresses his hair with art, and whoever's loose toga flows with a flowing fold, and whoever shall come in our way, let him stand far off, that he may have no ground for suspicion, or take another road. So the god himself commands, so the great priestess has prophesied to me with inspired voice. She, when she is stirred by Bellona's frenzy, fears neither the fierce flame nor, in her madness, the twisted lashes; she herself, in her violence, slashes her own arms with the axe and, the blood pouring out, sprinkles the goddess, unharmed, and stands with her side pierced through by the spear, stands with her breast wounded, and sings the events that the great goddess foretells: "Spare to wrong the girl whom Love guards, lest you be sorry, after, to have learned it through great misfortune. Should he touch her, his wealth will slip away, as the blood from our wound, as this ash is scattered by the winds." And she told you, my Delia, of I know not what penalties; yet if you should err, I pray they may be light upon you. It is not for your own sake that I spare you, but your mother moves me, and the golden old woman conquers my anger. She brings you to me in the darkness and amid much fear, and silently, in secret, joins our hands, she waits for me by the doors at night, pressed close, and knows from afar the sound of my feet as I come. Live long for me, sweet old woman: with you I would gladly, if only it were lawful, have shared my own years. You I shall always love, and your daughter for your sake: whatever she does, she is still your own blood. Only teach her to be chaste, though no fillet binds her gathered hair, nor a long robe her feet. And let harsh laws be mine: let me not be able to praise any woman, but she will fly at my eyes, and if she thinks I have erred in anything, let me be dragged by the hair and thrown headlong, undeserving, through the streets. I would not wish to strike you, but if that madness should come, I would wish I had no hands; nor be chaste through cruel fear, but with a faithful heart: let mutual love, even in my absence, keep you for me. But she who has been faithful to no one, conquered by old age at last, draws out the twisted threads with a trembling hand, in want, and binds firm leashes to the hired loom and trims the drawn-out wool from the snowy fleece. The bands of young men watch her with rejoicing hearts and declare that the old woman deservedly bears so many ills, and Venus, lofty, looks upon her weeping from high Olympus and warns how bitter she is to the faithless. Let these curses fall on others; let us, Delia, be a pattern of love, both of us, even with grey hair.

Macer follows the camp: what will become of tender Love? Will he be a companion and bravely bear arms on his neck? And whether the long road of the lands or the wandering seas lead the man, will Love wish to go to his side with weapons? Burn, boy, I pray, the fierce one who has left your ease, and again call back the runaway beneath your standards. But if you spare soldiers, this one too will be a soldier, who carries the light water for himself in his helmet. I seek the camp, and farewell to Venus and farewell to girls: strength too is mine, and the trumpet is a joy to me. Great words I speak, but when I have grandly spoken great things, the closed doors shake the brave words out of me. How often have I sworn never to return to her threshold! When I have sworn it well, yet my foot of itself returns. Fierce Love, would that I might see your weapons broken, the arrows, and, if it be allowed, the torches put out! You torment my misery, you compel me to call down curses on myself and to speak unspeakable things with maddened mind. By now I would have ended my ills with death, but credulous Hope nurses my life and ever says tomorrow will be better. Hope feeds the farmers, Hope entrusts to the ploughed furrows the seeds that the field will repay with great interest: this catches birds with the snare, this fish with the rod, when the slender hooks have hidden the bait before: Hope too consoles the one bound with a stout fetter: his legs ring with iron, but he sings amid his work: Hope promises me an easy Nemesis, but she denies it. Ah me, do not conquer the goddess, hard girl. Spare me, I pray, by the untimely bones of your sister: so may the little one rest peacefully beneath the tender earth. Holy she is to me, to her tomb I will bring offerings, and garlands wet with my tears, to her mound I will flee and sit, a suppliant, and bewail my fate with the silent ashes. She will not endure that her client weep on and on for your sake: in her name I forbid you to be cold to me, lest the neglected shade send you evil dreams, and your mournful sister stand before your sleeping couch, such as she came, fallen headlong from the high window, bloodstained, down to the infernal pools. I cease, lest my mistress's bitter griefs be renewed: I am not worth so much that she should weep even once. Nor is she worthy to spoil her telltale eyes with tears: the bawd harms us, the girl herself is good. Phryne the bawd is murdering me, wretch, and stealthily carrying letters comes and goes with a hidden bosom: often, when from the hard threshold I recognize my mistress's sweet voice, this woman says she is not at home: often, when a night has been promised me, she announces the girl is unwell, or that she has taken fright at some threats. Then I die of cares, then my distracted mind imagines who holds my girl, or in how many ways he holds her: then, bawd, I call down curses on you: anxious enough may you live, if even the smallest part of my vows has moved the gods.

Radiant Liber, be present — so may the mystic vine be ever yours, so may you wear your temples bound with ivy — take away, you who heal, my grief along with the rest: often by your gift love has fallen, overcome. Dear boy, let the cups be wet with noble wine, and pour out the Falernian for us with a tilted hand. Go far off, you harsh tribe of cares, go, you labours; let the Delian shine here with his snow-white birds. Do you, sweet friends, only favour my purpose, and let no one refuse to be my comrade with me for leader, or if anyone declines the gentle contest of the wine, let his dear girl deceive him with hidden guile. That god makes spirits rich, that god crushes the fierce one and gives him over to his mistress's judgement, Armenian tigers and tawny lionesses he has conquered and given soft hearts to the untamed. This Love and greater things can do; but ask for the gifts of Bacchus: which of you do dry cups please? Liber consorts on equal terms, and is not grim toward those who cherish him and merry wine together, but he comes angry to the over-stern: let whoever fears the great powers of the angry god drink. What penalties, how great and how terrible, he threatens these, the bloody prey of the Cadmean mother teaches. But far from us let this fear be, and let her, if any such there be, feel what the wrath of the wronged god can do. But what do I pray, madman? Let the winds, let the airy clouds carry off my rash vows to be scattered. Although no care for me remains to you, Neaera, be happy, and may your fortunes be bright. But let us give our hours over to the carefree table: after many a day comes one that is serene. Ah me, it is hard to imitate false joys, hard to feign mirth with a cheerless mind, nor does laughter sit well on a lying face, nor do drunken words ring well from the troubled. Why do I complain, unhappy man? Shameful cares, depart: father Lyaeus hates cheerless words. Cnossian maid, you once wept for the perjuries of the Thesean tongue, left alone by an unknown sea: so the learned Catullus sang of you, daughter of Minos, recounting the impious deeds of the ungrateful man. Now I warn you, men: happy is whoever from another's grief shall learn to be able to guard against his own. Nor let arms hung about your neck capture you, nor let a foul tongue deceive you with coaxing faith; even if the deceiver has sworn by her own dear eyes, and by her Juno and by her Venus, no faith will be in it: Jupiter laughs at the perjuries of lovers and bids the winds carry them off unfulfilled. Why, then, do I so often complain of the words of a deceitful girl? Go from me, I pray, you grave words. How I would wish to rest with you the long nights and to lie awake with you through the long days, faithless one, and undeservedly my enemy though I deserve well, faithless, but, though faithless, dear still! Bacchus loves the Naiad: do you delay, slow attendant? Let the Marcian water temper the aged wine. I shall not, if a girl flees the feasts of our table, desiring in her folly an unknown bed, keep heaving sighs, troubled, all night long. You, boy, go, more boldly add the clear wine. Long since, my temples wet with Syrian spikenard, I ought to have twined my hair with garlands.

This day the Fates sang of, spinning the fated threads that no god may unravel, this day that should bring one who could rout the Aquitanian peoples, before whom the Atax, conquered by his brave soldiery, should tremble. It has come to pass: the Roman youth has seen new triumphs and leaders with captive arms bound; and you, Messalla, wearing the victorious laurels, the ivory chariot bore along with its gleaming horses. This honour was not won for you without me: Tarbellian Pyrene is witness, and the shores of the Santonic Ocean, witness the Saône and the swift Rhône and the great Garonne, and the dark-blue water of the Loire of the fair-haired Carnutes. Or shall I sing of you, Cydnus, who gently, with silent waters, dark-blue, glide along your calm channels through the shallows, and how great the cold Taurus, touching the clouds with its peak in the sky, nourishes the unshorn Cilicians? Why tell how the white dove, sacred to the Palestinian Syrian, flits unharmed through the crowded cities, and how Tyre, first taught to trust her ship to the winds, looks out from her towers over the vast level of the sea, and how the Nile, fertile, overflows with its summer water, when the Dog-star splits the parched fields? Father Nile, by what cause could I tell of you, or in what lands you have hidden your source? Because of you your land asks for no rains, nor does the dry grass entreat rain-bringing Jove. You the barbarous youth sing of and wonder at, as their Osiris, taught to mourn the Memphite bull. Osiris first made ploughs with skilful hand and stirred the tender earth with the iron, he first committed seeds to the untried soil and gathered fruits from unfamiliar trees. He taught how to join the tender vine to the stakes, how to cut the green foliage with the hard pruning-hook; for him the ripe grape, pressed by untrained feet, first gave its pleasant flavours. That liquor taught how to bend the voice in song and moved the unskilled limbs to fixed measures, Bacchus gave to the farmer's heart, worn out with great toil, release from its sadness. Bacchus brings rest to suffering mortals, though their legs ring, struck with the hard fetter. Cheerless cares and grief are not yours, Osiris, but the dance and song and light love befit you, and varied flowers and the brow wreathed with ivy-clusters, the yellow robe flowing down to the tender feet, and Tyrian garments and the sweet pipe with its song and the light basket, partner of the secret rites. Come hither, and grace the Genius with games and the Genius with dances, and drench your temples with much wine: let perfumes drip from his gleaming hair, and let him wear soft garlands on head and neck. So come, god of this day: to you I would give the honours of incense and bring sweet cakes with Mopsopian honey. But for you may offspring grow up, to increase your deeds, your child's deeds, and stand revered around you in your age. Nor let the land that Tusculum holds, and bright Alba with its ancient Lar, be silent of the monuments of the road. For with your wealth here the hard gravel is heaped and laid down, here the flint is joined with fitting skill. You the farmer sings of, when, late from the great city, he brings his foot home without stumbling. But you, Birthday, to be honoured through many years, come ever brighter and brighter.

Panegyric of Messalla You, Messalla, I shall sing, though your proven worth frights me; though my feeble strength cannot stand fast, yet I will begin, and if my songs fall short of the praises you deserve, — let me be a humble author for deeds so great, nor could anyone but you weave your deeds into his pages, such that no greater ones remain unspoken, — for me it is enough to have wished it; and do not spurn small gifts: even to Phoebus the most welcome offerings a Cretan brought, and to Bacchus the guest more pleasing than all was Icarus, as the stars in the clear sky bear witness, Erigone and the Dog, lest a later age deny it; nay, Alcides too, the god soon to ascend Olympus, set his glad steps in the cottage of Molorchus, and a little grain appeased the heavenly one, nor for them does the bull always fall a victim with gilded horn. Let this small labour too be welcome, so that I may be able to compose for you other verses, mindful, on another theme. Let another tell of the marvellous fabric of the great world, how the earth has settled in the boundless air, how the sea has flowed together into a curving orb, and the wandering air, where it strives to rise from the lands, and how the fiery ether, woven everywhere about it, flows, and how all things are shut within the overhanging sky; but whatever my Muses shall be able to dare, whether they can equal you or, what hope denies, go beyond, or fall short (and surely they will sing short), all this I vow to you, nor let my page lack so great a song. For though the praises of your ancient line abound to you, your glory is not content with the fame of your ancestors, nor do you ask what each label says beneath its image, but you strive to surpass the old honours of your race, yourself a greater glory to those to come than were your forebears to you: but a title beneath your name will not contain your deeds, but great volumes of eternal verse will be yours, and from every side, eager to compose your praises, they will gather, both those who sing in bound measure and those in free; which is better, there will be a contest: may I be victor among them, that I may inscribe my name upon deeds so great. For who achieves greater things than you in the camp or the forum? Yet here or there your praise is neither greater nor less, as when the just balance is pressed with equal weight, and sinks no more on this side nor rises from that, such as it floats unsteady, sunk lower on alternate sides, if ever an uneven load presses on either hand. For whether the inconstancy of the divided mob rage, no other could calm it; or if a judge's anger must be appeased, it can grow gentle at your words. Not Pylos or Ithaca is said to have borne such great men, Nestor or Ulysses, the great glory of a little city, though that old man lived while Titan ran thrice through the world's ages in his fruitful hours, though that one wandered, bold, through unknown cities, where the land is shut in by the sea's furthest waves: for he repelled the bands of the Cicones with opposing arms, nor could the lotus turn aside the courses he had begun, and the Neptunian dweller of the Aetnaean crag gave way, his eye disfigured, vanquished by Maronean wine; he carried the Aeolian winds over the peaceful sea, he came to the savage Laestrygonians and Antiphates, whom famed Artacie waters with her cold stream; he alone the cups of skilled Circe did not change, though she was the offspring of the Sun, apt with herbs and apt with song to change men's ancient shapes; he came too to the dark towers of the Cimmerians, to whom day never appeared with gleaming dawn, whether Phoebus ran above the lands or below; he saw how the great offspring of the gods, subjected to the infernal kingdom of Pluto, ran among the light shades, and passed the Sirens' shores with swift ship; him, swimming between the borders of a twofold death, neither did the onset of Scylla terrify with her savage mouth, when she crept with her dogs amid the raging waves, nor did violent Charybdis consume in her wonted way, whether she rose on high from the lowest swell, or laid bare the sea with the gulf cut open. Let not the violated pastures of the wandering Sun be passed in silence, nor the love and the fruitful fields of Atlantean Calypso, nor the end of his wretched wandering, the Phaeacian land. And whether these things are known among our own lands, or whether legend gave a new world to these wanderings, let his be the labour, while your eloquence is the greater. For now no other masters the arts of war more fitly than you: where it is fitting to draw a safe trench before the camp, how to fix the stakes against the enemy facing him, or what place is better closed off by a drawn rampart, where the earth may break forth sweet streams of water, how the approach may be easy for your men and hard for the enemy, how the soldier may flourish in the constant contest for praise, who can hurl the slow stake or the swift arrow better, or break the opposing ranks with the supple javelin, or who can rein in a swift horse with a tight bit and give the loosed reins to the slow one, and in turn now strive with a straight course, or, if it please, wheel about in a shorter, curving ring, who can guard himself with the shield, on right hand or left, whether the heavy onset of the spear come this way or that, or strike the marked spots with the swift sling. And when at once the contests of bold Mars come on and the lines prepare to clash with opposing standards, then you do not fail to set the order of the battle, whether there be need that the line stand in a square column, that the rank run down with even fronts, or it please to plan a twofold battle apart, that the right wing hold the left and the left the right, and the victory of the twin chances be twofold. But my songs do not wander among doubtful praises: for I sing of what was proved in wars. Witness for me is the brave soldier of conquered Iapydia, witness too the treacherous Pannonian, scattered everywhere upon the icy Alps, witness one born poor in the Arupine fields, whom, should anyone see how old age has not broken him, he would marvel less at the thrice-told ages of Pylian fame: for while the old man passes the seasons of a long life, Titan would renew a hundred fruitful years, yet swift himself he dares to mount his body upon a swift horse, and sits, its master, with strong reins. With you for leader the Dalmatian, not before turned to flight, submitted his free neck to the Roman chain. Nor yet will you be content with this: greater things than those achieved press upon you, as it has been made known to me by truthful signs, with which Amythaonian Melampus could not contend. For lately you had put on a robe gleaming with Tyrian weft on the rising day, the first of the fruitful year, when the Sun, more splendid, lifted his head from the clear waves and the discordant winds held back their fierce blasts, nor did the curving rivers drive their wonted courses, nay, even the rapid sea stood still with calm waves, no bird glided through the airy breezes, nor did the rough beast graze the dense woods, nay, mute silence was lavished upon your vows. Jupiter himself, borne through the void on his light chariot, was present, and left Olympus near to heaven, and lent an ear intent upon your prayers, and nodded assent to all with truthful head: the fire, heaped upon the altars, shone brighter above the piled offerings. Nay, with the god urging you, begin to set yourself to great undertakings; let your triumphs not be the same as others': not facing you in neighbouring warfare will Gaul detain you, nor Spain bold in its broad lands, nor the fierce land beset by the Theraean settler, nor where either the Nile or the royal water Choaspes flows forth, or where the rapid Gyndes, Cyrus's madness, or the Oroatian wave, dries up on the Araccaean plains, nor where Tomyris bounded her kingdom by the wandering Araxes, nor where the Padaean, neighbour to Phoebus, keeping impious feasts at his savage tables, holds the furthest fields, and where Hebrus and Tanais water the Getae and the Magyni. Why do I delay? Where Ocean encircles the world with its sea, no region will set itself against you in arms. The Briton awaits you, unconquered by Roman war, and the other half of the world, with the sun set between. For the earth stands fast in the air poured round it and is divided into five parts over the whole orb. And two are always laid waste by icy cold: there the earth is hidden in dense shadow, and no wave glides on, its flowing checked, but, hardened, it stiffens into dense ice and snow, since there Titan never drives his risings overhead. But the middle is always subject to the heat of Phoebus, whether nearer to the lands he is borne into the summer circle or swiftly hastens to run down the winter days; therefore the earth does not rise up under the pressing plough, nor do the crops yield fruit nor the lands their pasture; there no god tends the fields, neither Bacchus nor Ceres, and no living things dwell in the scorched parts. Between this and the frozen zones is set the fertile one, both ours and the other part opposite to our soil, which the like nearness of the sky on either side tempers, and the one air kills the other's force; hence the gentle year turns for us through the seasons, hence the bull has learned to bow his neck to the yoke and the pliant vine to climb the lofty boughs, and the yearly crop is reaped of its ripe fruits, and the earth is cleft with iron, the sea with bronze, nay, even towns rise up with built walls. Therefore when your deeds have gone through bright triumphs, you alone, the same, will be called great in either world. I am not enough for the heralding of so great a praise, not if Phoebus himself should write the songs for me. You have one who can gird himself for great matters, Valgius: no other is nearer to immortal Homer. My toil does not pass its time in languid ease, although Fortune, as is her way, wearies me, turned against me. For me, when my lofty house gleamed with great wealth, which had golden furrows in their rows to enrich it and barns scarce able to hold the fruitful harvest, and whose flocks the hills pastured in a dense throng, enough for the master, and too much for the thief and the wolf, now only longing remains: for the care is made new whenever, remembering, grief ever reminds me of years gone by. But though harsher things befall and I am stripped of what is left, my Muses will not fail to commemorate you. Nor to you alone will Pierian honours be paid: for you I would dare to go even over the swift waves of the sea, though the wintry straits swell with opposing winds, for you I would dare to stand alone against dense squadrons, or commit my small body to the Aetnaean flame. Whatever I am, it is yours.
