If a little care for me be yours, however much you please, if only there be any, not the Lydian kingdoms, not the fame of great Gylippus, would be more to me, nor would I rather be able to surpass the pages of Homer. But if my verse, all of it or less, be either well known to you, or float upon your lips, no fates will set for me an end of singing you. Nay, even when the mound shall have covered my bones, whether the ripe day hasten swift death for me, or long life remain, yet, my form changed, whether it fashion me a horse taught to course the stiff plains, or I be a bull, the glory of the slow herd, or I be borne, a bird, through the clear air on wings, whenever the long age shall receive me again as a man, I will weave songs of you upon pages newly begun.

I cannot be deceived as to what the nods of a lover, or what gentle words in a soft tone, may mean. For me there are no lots, no entrails privy to the gods' counsel, nor does the song of a bird foretell events for me: Venus herself, binding my arms with the magic knot, taught me thoroughly, not without many a blow. Cease to dissemble: the god burns more cruelly those whom he sees yield to him unwillingly. What does it now profit you to have tended your soft hair and so often to have arranged your changing locks, what to adorn your cheeks with gleaming rouge, what to have your nails trimmed by the practised hand of an artist? In vain now are your robes, in vain your mantles changed, and the tight band that binds your pressed-in feet. She pleases, though she has come with an unadorned face and has not dressed her shining head with slow art. Has some old woman bewitched you with chants, with pale herbs, in the silent hour of night? Chants draw the crops across from neighbouring fields, chants halt the course of the angry snake, chants even try to draw the Moon down from her chariot and would do it, if the clashing bronze did not resound. Why do I lament, alas, that a chant has harmed my wretched boy, why herbs? Beauty uses no magic aids: but to have touched the body harms, to have given long kisses, to have joined thigh to thigh. Yet remember, boy, not to be hard upon your girl: Venus pursues cheerless deeds with penalties. Do not demand gifts: let a grey-haired lover give gifts, that he may warm his cold limbs in a soft bosom. Dearer than gold is the youth whose smooth face gleams, and whose rough beard does not chafe the embrace. Beneath his shoulder set your gleaming arms, and let the great wealth of kings be despised. But Venus finds a way to lie with a boy in secret, while he fears, and presses close to the tender bosom, and to give moist kisses to him, panting, with battling tongues, and to fix the marks of teeth upon his neck. Stone and gem do not please her who must sleep alone in the cold and be desired by no man. Alas, too late is love recalled, too late youth, when grey old age has stained the white head. Then is there zeal for beauty: then the hair is changed, to hide the years, dyed with the green husk of a nut; then it is a care to pluck out the white hairs by the root and, the old skin removed, to bring back a new face. But you, while the bloom of your first season flowers for you, use it: it slips away with no slow foot. And do not torment Marathus: what glory is there in a conquered boy? Be hard upon old men, my girl. Spare the tender one, I pray: his is no serious ailment, but excessive love stains his body with paleness. How often, poor boy, does he fling cheerless complaints at her in her absence, and all things are wet and full of tears! "Why do you scorn me?" he says. "The guard could have been overcome: the god himself granted to the eager the power to deceive. Stolen love is known to me, how the breath may be drawn softly, how kisses snatched may give no sound; and I can creep up even in the middle of the night and unbar the doors in secret with no noise. What use are arts, if the cruel girl scorns her wretched lover and flees from the very bed? Or when she promises, but suddenly, faithless, deceives me, then must I keep a night awake amid many ills. While I imagine she is coming, whatever stirs, I believe then that her feet have made the sound." Cease to weep, boy: she is not to be broken, and now your eyes, weary with weeping, are swollen. The gods hate disdain, Pholoe, I warn you, nor does it profit to have given incense to their holy hearths. This Marathus once made sport of wretched lovers, not knowing that an avenging god stood behind his head; often too he is said to have laughed at the tears of one in grief and to have held off the eager one with feigned delay: now he hates all haughtiness, now there displeases him whatever door is barred hard against him. But punishment awaits you, unless you cease to be proud. How you will wish, with prayers, to call back this day!

Elegies of Sulpicia by an Uncertain Author Sulpicia is dressed for you, great Mars, on your Kalends; come yourself from heaven to behold her, if you are wise; this Venus will forgive; but you, violent one, beware lest your arms fall shamefully from you as you marvel: from her eyes, when he wishes to set the gods aflame, keen Love kindles his twin torches. Her, whatever she does, wherever she has moved her steps, Grace secretly arrays and follows close behind; if she has loosed her hair, it is fitting to wear it flowing: if she has dressed it, with dressed locks she is to be revered. She kindles, whether she has chosen to come forth in a Tyrian robe: she kindles, whether she comes radiant in snow-white raiment. Such on eternal Olympus is happy Vertumnus, who has a thousand adornments, has a thousand fittingly. She alone of girls is worthy that Tyre should give her soft fleeces twice steeped in costly dyes, and that she should possess whatever the rich Arab reaps, the tiller of the fragrant crop, in his sweet-smelling fields, and whatever gems the dark Indian, nearest the Eastern waters, gathers from the red shore. Of her, you Pierian Maids, sing on the festal Kalends, and you, Phoebus, proud with your tortoise-shell lyre. This solemn rite she will keep for many years to come: no girl is worthier of your choir.

If you meant to wound my wretched love, why did you give pledges by the gods, to be broken in secret? Ah, wretch, even if at first one hides his perjuries, yet late comes Punishment with silent feet. Spare him, you of heaven: it is just that the beautiful be allowed, once, to wrong your powers unpunished. Seeking gain, the countryman yokes his bulls to the handy plough and presses the hard labour of the earth, seeking gain, the fixed stars guide the unsteady ships that will seek profit over the seas obedient to the winds: my boy was captured by gifts, but may the god turn those gifts to ashes and flowing waters. Soon he will pay me the penalty, and the dust will strip away his beauty and his hair grow rough in the winds; his face will be burnt, his hair burnt by the sun, and the long road will wear away his weak feet. How often I warned him: "Do not defile your beauty with gold: often many evils lie hidden beneath gold. If anyone, captured by riches, has violated love, Venus is harsh and unkind to him. Rather burn my head with flame and strike my body with the sword and cut my back with the twisted lash. And let there be no hope of hiding it for one preparing to sin: there is a god who forbids that deceits should stay secret. The god himself allowed the silent servant to speak softly, to utter free words over much wine; the god himself bade those mastered by sleep to send forth their voice and, against their will, to speak of deeds that should be hidden." These things I used to say: now I am ashamed to have wept as I spoke, now to have fallen at your tender feet. Then you swore to me that for no weight of rich gold, for no gems, would you sell your faith, not if the land of Campania were given you as a price, not if Falernian fields, the care of Bacchus, were yours. With those words you would have torn from me the belief that the stars of heaven shine, and that the paths of the lightning are clear. You even wept: but I, not skilled in deceit, credulous, kept wiping the tears from your wet cheeks. What was I to do, but that you too were in love with a girl? Yet I pray she may be fickle to you, after your own example. O how often, that no one might be privy to our words, I myself, your companion, carried the torch through the deep night! Often, by my gift, she came to you when you did not hope for it and hid behind the closed doors, veiled. Then I, wretched, was undone, fool that I was to trust I was loved: for I might have been more wary of your snares. What is more, with stunned mind I sang your praises, and now I am ashamed of myself and of the Muses. I would that Vulcan might scorch those songs with rapid flame and the river wash them away with its flowing water. You, keep far from here, whose care is to sell your beauty and carry back great profit with a full hand. But you, who dared to corrupt the boy with gifts, may your wife mock you, unavenged, with constant tricks, and when she has wearied a youth with stolen pleasure, let her lie down beside you, languid, with a robe between. Let there always be strangers' traces in your bed, and let your house always lie open to the eager; nor let her wanton sister be said to have drunk more cups, or to have served more men. They say she often draws out the feasts with Bacchus, until the risen wheel of the Morning Star summons the day. No woman could spend the night better than she or arrange the various changes of her tasks. But your wife has learned all this, and you, most foolish, do not perceive it, when she moves her body for you with unwonted art. Do you think she dresses her hair for you or combs her fine locks with the close-toothed comb? Is it that face that persuades, to bind her arms with gold and come forth fitted out in a Tyrian fold? Not for you, but for some young man she wishes to look fine, for whose sake she would curse both your fortune and your house. Nor does she do this from vice, but the elegant girl flees bodies foul with gout and an old man's embrace. Yet beside this man our boy has lain: him I could believe able to join in love with savage beasts. Have you dared to sell my coaxing words to others? Have you, madman, dared to carry my kisses to others? Then you will weep, when another boy holds me bound and reigns in proud sovereignty over your kingdom. But then your punishment will gladden me, and to deserving Venus a golden palm, fixed up, shall mark my fortunes: "Freed from a deceitful love, Tibullus dedicates this to you, and asks, goddess, that you be of gracious mind."

Spare my young man, whether you haunt the good pastures of the plain or the byways of the shady mountain, you boar, and let it not be yours to have whetted your hard tusks for battle; let Love, his guardian, keep him safe for me. But the love of hunting leads him far away, Delia: O perish the woods, and let the hounds fail! What madness is it, what sense, with the net to close the dense hills, wishing to hurt his tender hands? Or what pleasure is it to steal into the lairs of wild beasts and to mark his white legs with the hooked brambles? Yet, that it might be allowed to wander with you, Cerinthus, I myself would carry the twisted nets over the mountains, I myself would seek the tracks of the swift stag and take the iron bonds from the swift hound. Then, then the woods would please me, if, my light, with you I might be charged with having lain before the very snares: then, though the boar come to the toils, it will go off unharmed, that it may not disturb the joys of eager love. Now without me let there be no love, but by Diana's law, chaste boy, touch the chaste nets with a chaste hand: and whatever woman steals secretly upon my love, let her fall among the savage beasts, to be torn apart. But you, yield your zeal for hunting to your father, and run swiftly yourself back into my arms.

Who was it that first brought forth dreadful swords? How fierce and truly iron-hearted that man was! Then slaughter was born to the race of men, then battles, then a shorter road to dread death was opened. Or did that wretch deserve no blame, but did we turn to our own harm what he gave against savage beasts? This is the fault of rich gold, nor were there wars when a beechwood cup stood before the feasts. There were no citadels, no rampart, and the leader of the flock sought sleep untroubled among his scattered sheep. Then I should have lived, nor would I have known the cheerless arms of the mob, nor heard the trumpet with a quaking heart; now I am dragged to war, and now perhaps some enemy carries the weapon that will lodge in my side. But guard me, my fathers' Lares: you nourished me, the same, when as a child I ran about before your feet. And be not ashamed to be made of an old stump: so you dwelt in the home of my forefather of old. Then men kept faith better, when, in poor worship, the wooden god stood in his little shrine. He was appeased, whether someone had offered the grape or laid garlands of grain on his holy hair, and one, his prayer fulfilled, himself brought the cakes, and after him his little daughter brought the clear honeycomb. But from us, Lares, ward off the bronze weapons, . . . . . . and a country pig from the full sty as victim. This I shall follow in clean garments, and bound with myrtle I shall bear the baskets, bound with myrtle on my own head too. So may I please you: let another be brave in arms and lay low the enemy leaders with Mars to favour him, that, while I drink, the soldier may tell me his deeds and trace his camp in wine upon the table. What madness is it to summon black death by war? It hangs over us and comes in secret on silent foot. Below there is no crop, no cultivated vineyard, but bold Cerberus and the foul ferryman of the Stygian water; there, with bruised cheeks and burnt hair, the pale throng wanders by the gloomy pools. How much rather to be praised is he whom, his offspring assured, slow old age overtakes in his little cottage. He himself follows his sheep, his son the lambs, and his wife makes ready warm water for him when he is weary. So may I be, and may it be allowed that my head grow white with age and that, an old man, I tell of the deeds of former times. Meanwhile let Peace tend the fields. Bright Peace first led the oxen to plough beneath the curved yoke, Peace nourished the vines and stored up the juice of the grape, that the father's jar might pour out wine for the son, in Peace the hoe and the ploughshare gleam—but rust seizes in the darkness the cheerless arms of the hard soldier— and the countryman, none too sober himself, brings home from the grove his wife and his children in the wagon. But then the wars of Venus grow hot, and the woman laments her torn hair and her broken-down doors. She weeps, her tender cheeks bruised, but the victor himself weeps that his maddened hands had such strength. But wanton Love supplies the bitter words to the quarrel, and sits, indifferent, between the two angry ones. Ah, he is stone and iron, whoever strikes his girl: he drags the gods down from heaven. Let it be enough to tear the thin robe from her limbs, let it be enough to undo the ordering of her hair, let it be enough to have moved her to tears: four times blessed is he at whom a tender girl can weep when he is angry. But let him who is savage with his hands bear shield and stake, and let him stay far from gentle Venus. But to us, kindly Peace, come, and hold the corn-ear, and let your bright bosom be overflowing with fruits in front.

Come hither and drive out the sickness of the tender girl, come hither, Phoebus, proud of your unshorn hair; believe me, make haste, nor will you regret it now, Phoebus, to have laid your healing hands upon a lovely woman. Bring it about that no wasting seize her pallid limbs, nor any disfiguring hue mark her white body, and whatever of ill there is, and whatever cheerless thing we fear, let the river bear it away to the sea with its rushing waters. Holy one, come, and bring with you whatever flavours, whatever chants ease wearied bodies; nor torment the young man, who fears the girl's death and makes vows for his mistress scarce to be numbered; now and then he vows, now and then, because she is ill, he speaks harsh words against the eternal gods. Lay aside your fear, Cerinthus: the god does not harm lovers; only love always: your girl is safe for you; there is no need of weeping: it will be fitter to use your tears if ever she shall be more downcast toward you. But now she is wholly yours, she, radiant, thinks of you alone with herself, and the credulous crowd sits in vain. Phoebus, show favour: great praise will be paid to you to have saved two in one body kept safe. Now you will be famed, now glad, when each, glad, in rivalry pays back what is owed to your holy hearths; then the pious throng of gods will call you happy, and each will wish your arts for himself.

The day that gave you to me, Cerinthus, this shall be holy to me, and ever to be counted among the festal days: at your birth the Fates sang to girls a new slavery, and gave to you proud sovereignty. I burn before all others: this pleases me, Cerinthus, that I burn, if from you a mutual fire toward me is present; let mutual love be present, I ask by our sweetest stolen joys, and by your eyes, and by your Genius. Great Genius, take the incense gladly and favour my vows, if only, when he thinks of me, he glows. But if perchance he now sighs for other loves, then, holy one, leave, I pray, those faithless hearths. And do not be unjust, Venus: either let each serve you, bound alike, or lift the bonds from me; but rather let both of us be held by a strong chain, which no day hereafter could loose. The young man wishes the same as I, but wishes it more secretly: for he is ashamed to speak these words openly. But you, Birthday god, since you perceive all things as a god, grant it: what does it matter whether he ask in secret or openly?

Birthday Juno, take the holy heaps of incense that the skilled girl gives you with her tender hand; today she is wholly yours, for you she has dressed herself most gladly, that she might stand, fair to behold, before your hearths. She indeed refers to you, goddess, the causes of her adorning; yet there is one whom she would secretly wish to please. But you, holy one, show favour, and let no one tear the lovers apart, but for the young man, I beg, prepare equal bonds. So you will match them well: not to any girl is he worthier to be a slave, nor she to any man. And let no watchful guard be able to catch the eager pair, and let Love supply a thousand ways of deceiving. Grant it, and come, shining through your purple robe: three times a cake is offered you, three times, chaste goddess, wine; the eager mother instructs her daughter in what she wishes: the girl now, silent, in her own heart asks another thing; she burns, as the swift flames burn the altars, nor, though she might, would she wish to be whole again. Be gracious to the young man, and, when the next year comes, let this same love stand firm, now grown old in its vows.

Little Elegies of Sulpicia At last love has come, of such a kind that to have veiled it would be more a shame to me, by repute, than to have laid it bare to anyone. Won over by my Muses, the Cytherean goddess brought him and laid him in my bosom. Venus has paid her promises: let one tell of my joys, if any shall be said not to have had her own. I would not wish to entrust anything to sealed tablets, that no one might read it before my own beloved, but it is a delight to have erred; to compose my looks for repute's sake wearies me: let me be told to have been worthy, with one worthy of me.

The hated birthday is at hand, which must be spent, cheerless, in the wearisome country and without Cerinthus. What is sweeter than the city? Or is a farmhouse fit for a girl, and the cold river of the Arretine field? Now, Messalla, too zealous for me, be at rest; journeys, kinsman, are often not timely. Carried off, I leave here my mind and my senses to my own will, though you do not let me be my own.

Do you know that the cheerless journey has been lifted from the girl's mind? Now I may be at Rome on your birthday. Let that birthday be kept by us all, which now comes to you by chance, when you do not expect it.

It is pleasing that, untroubled, you now grant yourself so much about me, lest I, suddenly, in my folly, fall to ruin. Let your care be rather for the toga, and a harlot weighed down with the wool-basket, than Sulpicia, daughter of Servius: they are anxious on my behalf, to whom this is the greatest cause of grief, that I should yield to an ignoble bed.

Have you, Cerinthus, any loyal care for your girl, now that a fever vexes my wearied body? Ah, I would not wish to overcome my cheerless sickness otherwise than if I thought that you too wished it. But what would it profit me to overcome my sickness, if you can bear my ills with an indifferent heart?

May I no longer be, my light, so fervent a care to you as I seem to have been a few days before, if in all my youth I, foolish, have done anything of which I should confess I have repented more than that I left you alone last night, desiring to hide my own ardour.

By an Uncertain Author No woman shall steal your bed from me: on this terms first was our love joined. You alone please me, nor now, besides you, in the city is any girl lovely to my eyes. And would that you could seem fair to me alone! May you displease others: so shall I be safe. There is no need of envy, let the glory of the crowd be far off: let the man who is wise rejoice in a silent breast. So can I live well in the secret woods, where no path is worn by human foot. You are the rest from my cares, you in the black night are my light, and in lonely places you are a throng to me. Now though a sweetheart be sent from heaven to Tibullus, she would be sent in vain, and Venus would fail; this I swear to you by the holy power of your Juno, who alone before all other gods is great to me. What am I doing, madman? Alas! alas! I yield up my pledges; I have sworn foolishly: that fear was to my profit. Now you will be bold, now more daringly you will burn me: this my chattering tongue has brought as ill upon my wretched self. Now I will do whatever you wish, I will remain yours forever, nor will I flee the slavery of a well-known mistress, but, bound, I will sit at holy Venus's altars: she marks the unjust and favours suppliants.
Rumour says again and again that my girl is false: now I would wish to be of deaf ears. These charges are not made without grief to me: why do you torment a wretch, bitter Rumour? Be silent.

Of Domitius Marsus You too, Tibullus, the comrade of Virgil, unjust Death sent, a young man, to the Elysian fields, that there might be none either to weep tender loves in elegy or to sing royal wars in heroic measure.
